subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f(x) = tan⁻¹((√(1 + x²) − 1)/x) and g(x) = tan⁻¹x, differentiate f(x) with respect to g(x).

mark_split.label: Simplify f(x) with x = tan θ

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what differentiating f with respect to g means, and what substitution you would use.

steps.label: State what df/dg means
steps.margin_note: First mark. This one line decides the question. A student who differentiates f alone and stops loses every mark after this.
lines: To differentiate one function with respect to another,

accept: differentiate f with respect to g means f dash over g dash
divide the derivative of f by the derivative of g
it is not d f by d x, it is d f by d g
f dash ni g dash tho divide cheyyali
both are differentiated with respect to x first and then divided

steps.why: The question does not ask for df/dx. Writing the rule first fixes exactly what has to be computed and earns the method mark.
common_mistakes: Giving df/dx as the final answer.
Writing df/dg = (dg/dx)/(df/dx), the two the wrong way round.
steps.memory_tip: Read df/dg as (df/dx) ÷ (dg/dx) — the dx cancels, which shows the fraction is the right way up.

steps.label: Simplify f(x) with x = tan θ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. θ = Tan⁻¹x lies in (−π/2, π/2), so θ/2 lies in (−π/4, π/4) and Tan⁻¹(tan(θ/2)) is exactly θ/2.
lines: Put x = tan θ, so θ = Tan⁻¹x and √(1 + x²) = sec θ
(√(1 + x²) − 1)/x = (sec θ − 1)/tan θ = (1 − cos θ)/sin θ

recall.must_convey: That putting x = tan θ collapses f(x) to θ/2, that is, f(x) = ½ Tan⁻¹x.
accept: put x equal to tan theta and f becomes theta by two
f of x is half of tan inverse x
sec theta minus one over tan theta is tan of theta by two
x ni tan theta ga pettite f theta by two avuthundi
the bracket simplifies to tan of half the angle

steps.why: The bracket is not a standard derivative, so it is simplified first. Under x = tan θ it becomes tan(θ/2), and the inverse tangent then cancels the tangent.
common_mistakes: Writing √(1 + x²) as sec²θ instead of sec θ.
Cancelling the 1 in (√(1 + x²) − 1)/x term by term.
steps.memory_tip: (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = tan(θ/2), because 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2) and sin θ = 2 sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2).

steps.label: Differentiate f and g
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Both derivatives use d/dx(Tan⁻¹x) = 1/(1 + x²); only the constant ½ separates them.

accept: f dash is one over two into one plus x squared
g dash is one over one plus x squared
the derivative of tan inverse x is one over one plus x squared
tan inverse x derivative one by one plus x square
f dash is half of g dash

steps.why: Once f is written as ½ Tan⁻¹x, both derivatives come from the same standard result, so there is nothing left to simplify.
common_mistakes: Dropping the ½ from f and getting 1 instead of ½ at the end.
steps.memory_tip: f is exactly half of g, so f′ must be exactly half of g′ — check the ½ survives.

steps.label: Divide the two derivatives
steps.margin_note: Last mark. A constant answer is the check that the substitution was right: f is half of g everywhere, so their rates stay in the fixed ratio 1 : 2.

recall.must_convey: That the (1 + x²) factors cancel and df/dg = 1/2, a constant.
accept: one plus x squared cancels and the answer is one half
the answer is a constant one by two
divide f dash by g dash to get half
answer constant, one by two vasthundi
getting a constant shows the substitution was correct

steps.why: The answer is independent of x, and that is the check on the working: f and g differ only by the factor ½, so no x can survive.
common_mistakes: Leaving x in the final answer, which means the simplification in step 2 was not completed.
Giving 2 instead of 1/2 by dividing the wrong way round.
steps.memory_tip: Test it at x = 1: f(1) = π/8 and g(1) = π/4, and π/8 is half of π/4.

insider_note: f simplifies to ½Tan⁻¹x under x = tan θ, so f′ is exactly half of g′. The ratio df/dg is the constant ½, and simplifying f before differentiating is what makes that visible.
